text: Let's close out the landscape chapter by putting everything together: the exact same task, written correctly in five different dialects, side by side. The task is simple -- get the five highest-priced products from a table.

In T-SQL, you'd write select top open-paren five close-paren, then order by list price descending. In Oracle SQL, it's select, order by, then fetch first five rows only -- the newer standard syntax. Notice everything except that one clause is essentially the same query.

MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Snowflake all happen to agree with each other here -- all three use limit five at the end, with an otherwise identical query. Three different platforms, one shared syntax, purely by convention rather than any technical requirement.

So the only real difference across all five dialects, for this task, is three ways of saying "just the top N rows": T-SQL's proprietary top, Oracle's modern standard fetch first rows only, and the limit keyword shared by MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Snowflake.

This is the pattern to expect for the rest of the course. Basic querying is almost a non-issue -- it's nearly identical everywhere. The real differences live in data types, pagination detail, and especially procedural code, where the standard never fully standardized anything.

You now have the landscape: the players, how to set them up, how to read their docs, and a feel for where they agree. Chapter two starts digging into where they genuinely diverge, beginning with string types -- varchar, nvarchar, text, and clob. See you there.
